#This script: yearly analysis:

1.a Calculates distance between centroids of migrants and residents in each ecoregion to ask whether migrants and residents differ in their average trait combinations
1.b Calcualtes the distribution of species from the other group centroid to ask which migrants/residents are most unique to their group and thus which migrants are most unique in their contribution to the resident ecoregional pool
1.c. Calculates the distribution of species from their own group centroid to ask whether migrants/residents are unique within their group- if these match the species unique also compared to residents, suggets completely unique
1.d Further, the degree of specialisation (sum of euclidean distances from 5 nearest neighbours) and uniqueness (distance from centroid) of each species species from the (full ecoregional centroid) is calculated to ask whether species are unique irrespective of status group and then model migratory status ~ fucntional irreplaceability (functional specilisation x uniqueness) + (1|species) + (1|resident)
2.a Calculates the nestedness vs turnover of migrant vs resident groups to ask how much redundancy there in trait space occupancy between migrants and residents and to identify cases where migrant groups are simply complete subsets of the residents
2.b May calculate the distribution of nestedness vs turnover in each ecoregion as binary output i.e. to identify which species are nested and which are unique to the group
3. To understand which niches migrant and resident species are occupying in a more nuanced way,, I then define the niche in an Aristolelian rather than Hutchosonian way which quantitifies the essential (niche defined based on intrinsic functional traits e.g. defining niche based on speficic morphologies) rather than fundamental niche of a species (the set of conditions in which a species can persist)
This could be done using Avoniche to create subsets of each foraging niche, extract the PC scores for each subset from the full ecological space and map this onto morphspace as quantiles
Then distance to the quantiles of each niche for each species could be calculated then modelled as a function of migratory status. I.e. are migrants more invetivore than residents for example- then can infer how likely migrants are to outcompete residents within these niches!
niches to look at could be picked based on the tails of the boostrapped distribution i.e. the interesting niches that migrants only occupy, and the more generalist niches that both resident and migrants occupy 

#same for seasonal analysis with each ecoregional seasonal migrant and resident group compared 
#same for monthly (short stay vs long stay species) analysis with each ecoregional monthly migrant and resident group compared (potentially yearly and then seasonally)

## load packages
library(dispRity)


## load functions---------

```{r}
# making groups function
make.ecoregional.migrant.groups <- function(traitspace_df, by) {
  lapply(split(traitspace_df$species, traitspace_df[by], drop = TRUE), unique) # get list of species per ecoregion, status (and season for seasonal analysis) by splitting dataframe
}

# calcualting distance between centroids function
pairwise.distance.between.centroids <- function(matrix, matrix2) {
  ## calculate the centroid of the matrices of n-dimensional traitspace
  sqrt(sum((colMeans(matrix) - colMeans(matrix2))^2))
}

# calculating quantile overlap function (proportional overlap, does not identify nestedness only how much of traitspace is common to BOTH groups) so a good start- i.e. can answer, are groups occupying different or common areas of trait space?
quantile.overlap <- function(matrix, matrix2, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)) {
  q1 <- apply(matrix, 2, quantile, probs = probs)
  q2 <- apply(matrix2, 2, quantile, probs = probs)
  intersect <- pmax(0, pmin(q1[2, ], q2[2, ]) - pmax(q1[1, ], q2[1, ]))
  span <- pmax(q1[2, ], q2[2, ]) - pmin(q1[1, ], q2[1, ])
  intersect / span
}

# calculating turnover of a group relative to the other group: i.e. what proportion of traits are unique to the group? comparisons are pairwise
quantile.uniqueness <- function(matrix, matrix2, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)) {
  q1 <- apply(matrix, 2, quantile, probs = probs)
  q2 <- apply(matrix2, 2, quantile, probs = probs)
  intersect <- pmax(0, pmin(q1[2, ], q2[2, ]) - pmax(q1[1, ], q2[1, ])) # if no intersect, defualts to 0
  span <- q1[2, ] - q1[1, ]
  turnover <- span - intersect

  return(turnover / span)
}

# calculating nestedness of a group relative to the other group: i.e. what proportion of traits are simply a subset of the other group? comparisons are pairwise
quantile.nestedness <- function(matrix, matrix2, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)) {
  q1 <- apply(matrix, 2, quantile, probs = probs)
  q2 <- apply(matrix2, 2, quantile, probs = probs)
  intersect <- pmax(0, pmin(q1[2, ], q2[2, ]) - pmax(q1[1, ], q2[1, ]))
  span <- q1[2, ] - q1[1, ]

  return(intersect / span)
}

# calculating distribution of species' distances from the other groups centroid 
distribution.of.species.from.other.group.centroid <- function(matrix, matrix2) {
    ## calculate the centroid of the matrices of n-dimensional traitspace
  dist<- point.dist(matrix, matrix2) #euclidean distance from each species in group1 to the centroid of group2
  
} #returns 1 distance value for each element (species)
```



##Load traitspace and convert to matrix------------------------

```{r}
traitspace_df <- read.csv("Data/Processed/eco_region_season_traitspace_PCA_BI.csv")

pc_cols <- names(traitspace_df)[8:13] # get names of PC columns excluding metadata
species_pcs <- unique(traitspace_df[c("species", pc_cols)]) # get unique pc cols per species # i.e. the full trait space, 1 row per species

# convert to matrix for disprity
traitspace_mat <- as.matrix(species_pcs[, pc_cols])
rownames(traitspace_mat) <- species_pcs$species
```

## yearly analysis: do migrants vs residents differ in funtional contribution to the year round traitspace?----------

#see ellipse plots for preliminary plotting (mostly small overlaps, close to circle in a circle situation (see nestedness below))

#call function to split groups by ecoregion and migratory status
groups_yearly   <- make.ecoregional.migrant.groups(traitspace_df =traitspace_df, by = c("ecoregion", "status")) #disprity is calculated relative to the full trait space, i.e. what is the disprity of the ecoregional migrant vs resident group in the full Britain and Ireland traitspace. so will be regional for each region.- can compare biomes across a region but not across multiple regions (as will be different traitspaces)


#feed into custom subsets
subsets_yearly  <- custom.subsets(traitspace_mat, group = groups_yearly) #make subsets


#visualise
plot(subsets_yearly, type ="preview") #PC1 V2


plot(subsets_yearly, type="preview", specific.args = list(dimensions = c(3,4))) #PC1 v3

#boot and rarefy subsets to minimum species richness in any group for comparable ecoregional/season/migratory status comparisons
boot_yearly<- boot.matrix(subsets_yearly, bootstraps = 100, rarefaction = "min") #bootstrap with replacement (resample species from ecoregional pool for each migrant group and rarefy to the minimum number of species of a group in the ecoregion


disp_result<- dispRity(boot_yearly, metric = pairwise.distance.between.centroids, between.groups = TRUE) 
# this will compare each migrant and resident group within each ecoregion, can adapt using between.groups later on to include other cross-ecoregional checks

#caveat--------------
#when intepreting the resulkts can you see a clear effect- if yes probably does not need null hypothesis testign, if no then probably does
#therefore significance testing with p value provides statistical clarity- (Dushoff et al., 2019) argue this is the reason for performing p value testing ui.e. to provide clarity when you cannot "clearly see the result"
#e.g. if p<0.05 = “did not find a statistically clear effect.”  rather than no stastically significant effect (p values can be misleading because just because something is significant doesnt mean it is a large effetc or there is not a lot of noise around it, also the effect refers to a dataset not a study system)
#always important to report the effect size and confidence interval alongside the p vlaue (even if the confidence intervals are artifical i.e. from boostrapping), could also report observed and then the boostrapped values with confidence intervals
